label: 01 / Bit patterns
title: A number has a layout.
subtitle: HW 1–2 / Custom floating point
summary: Separate sign, exponent and fraction, then watch a hexadecimal word become a value.
work: My HW1 converts −5.375 into 0xCAC0, then decodes 0x3400 as 0.75 with bias 7 and 0.375 with bias 8. HW2 rounds the largest positive value to 511.88 and the exponent-one example to 0.0156.
review: Those values agree with the course's normalized 1/4/11 field model. Its exponent policy differs from IEEE binary16: the maximum calculation uses exponent 15 as finite. This new decoder explicitly uses the course formula for every field pattern; it does not implement IEEE zeros, subnormals, infinity or NaN.
steps: Convert 5.375 to 101.011₂.
Normalize to 1.01011₂ × 2² and add bias 7 to get exponent 9.
Pack sign 1, exponent 1001, fraction 01011000000.
Group into nibbles: 1100 1010 1100 0000 = CAC0.

label: 02 / Gate bench
title: Follow the signal.
subtitle: HW 2–3 / Boolean logic, full adder and mux
summary: Toggle inputs, compare a NAND-only circuit, and connect a truth-table row to a live gate diagram.
work: My HW2 proves the displayed De Morgan identity with matching truth tables, then converts x·not(y)+y·z into NAND gates. HW3 builds a full adder and a mux with output y when S=0 and x when S=1.
review: The full-adder equations S=A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout=AB+A·Cin+B·Cin are correct. The parity K-map's diagonal-looking group outlines do not represent valid adjacent SOP groups: parity ones are isolated. The XOR equation remains correct. The new circuits implement the stated equations, rather than certifying every hand-drawn connection.
steps: Build the truth table for every input combination.
Use XOR for odd parity and a majority function for carry.
For the mux, gate y with not(S), gate x with S, then OR the paths.
For NAND conversion, invert y with tied inputs; NAND the two product terms, then NAND their outputs.

label: 03 / Logisim files
title: A circuit remembers.
subtitle: Three original .circ files / Storage and routing
summary: Inspect reconstructed source wiring, download the native circuits, and compare a transparent latch with an edge-triggered register.
work: The archive contains D_flipflop.circ, Flip_flop.circ and dfunflop.circ. Their XML stores component types, labels, wire coordinates and Logisim source version 2.7.1. These are original files, not screenshot-only evidence.
review: D_flipflop.circ is a gated NAND D-latch structure despite its name. Flip_flop.circ has a gated NOR SR-latch structure. dfunflop.circ contains a mux and a separate built-in D flip-flop experiment. The source drawing below preserves wire endpoints with simplified component symbols; the behavior bench is a new ideal model, not a Logisim engine or exact electrical/delay simulation.
steps: A combinational circuit depends on the present inputs.
A latch is transparent during its enabled level, then holds its value.
A rising-edge flip-flop samples only at a 0-to-1 clock transition.
Real hardware also needs setup, hold and clock-to-Q timing; this model shows logical events only.

label: 04 / State machines
title: Recognize a pattern over time.
subtitle: HW 4–5 / Moore and Mealy recognizers
summary: Step through encoded states, compare output timing, and inspect the original state diagrams and circuits.
work: HW4 develops nonoverlapping 101 recognizers as Moore and Mealy machines, with state encoding, tables, equations and gate/register sketches. It also draws an overlapping Moore 1001 recognizer. HW5 adds a Mealy 1001 diagram.
review: The new reference models use explicit tables. Moore output is shown for the state entered after the sample; Mealy output is shown on the transition that consumed the bit. For 1001, the reference preserves a trailing 1 so two occurrences in 1001001 can share that boundary symbol. The faint labels and every derived SOP/gate edge are not fully certified.
steps: Let each state represent the longest useful pattern prefix.
Assign binary codes to the states.
For each state and input, determine the next state and output.
Implement next-state logic feeding D flip-flops, with state feedback into the logic.

label: 05 / Timing & NRZI
title: The clock follows the longest path.
subtitle: HW 5–6 / Delays, pipeline and encoding
summary: Compare datapath periods and pipeline schedules, then turn a binary word into an NRZI waveform.
work: HW6 calculates periods 2.85 ns, 2.15 ns and 1.25 ns, giving about 350.88, 465.12 and 800 MHz. It then uses 3N/(N+2) to estimate speedup as 2.99. The extra-credit work includes a five-state NRZI graph, table, equations and circuit.
review: The stated periods match the shown path assumptions. With unequal periods, actual single-versus-pipeline speedup for N=1000 is 2850/1252.5≈2.275, rather than the ideal equal-stage 2.994. The multi-cycle figure needs four cycles per result. NRZI needs only two level states; the reference defaults to right-to-left input and initial level 1, reproducing CF0C→EFAE.
steps: For one register-to-register path, add launch clock-to-Q, combinational delay, capture setup and the assigned skew allowance.
A single-cycle result crosses all three arithmetic modules.
Pipelining separates the modules, making the slowest stage set the period.
The first result takes three cycles; N results take N+2 cycles when no stalls occur.

label: 06 / Memory bus
title: Bits per transfer become bandwidth.
subtitle: HW 7 / Memory organization and timing
summary: Adjust bus width and clock rate, compare SDR with DDR, and inspect an explanatory memory-read waveform.
work: My HW7 computes 800 MB/s for 32-bit SDR at 200 MHz, 1600 MB/s for 64-bit SDR, and 1600 MB/s for 32-bit DDR. It also discusses the CPU, control signals and memory cycles.
review: The three peak bandwidth calculations are correct using decimal MB. Achieved throughput can be lower because of command overhead and other delays. Memory controllers issue the physical transactions, sometimes on behalf of CPUs or DMA devices. A quoted 1–4 CPU cycles is not a universal memory latency rule. The waveform is a new schematic explanation with no device-specific timing guarantee.
steps: Divide the data-bus width by eight to get bytes per transfer.
Multiply by transfers per clock: one for SDR, two for DDR.
Multiply by the clock rate in MHz to obtain decimal MB/s.
Separate peak bus throughput from access latency and real application throughput.

label: 07 / CPU workbench
title: Give each component a job.
subtitle: HW 8 / Accumulator datapath and RISC trace
summary: Select a datapath component to read my explanation, execute the required instruction types, and follow the six-line RISC example.
work: My submission draws an accumulator CPU datapath and explains PP, instruction memory, control, ACC, status, ALU, data memory and muxes. The RISC answer correctly leaves R4 at 5 after line 6, while R5 and memory A hold 125.
review: The interactive CPU is a new instruction-level reference: 16-bit data, 4-bit addresses and signed 4-bit immediate operands. It supports the nine requested operations but does not reconstruct undocumented opcode values or certify the hand-drawn decoder and every control wire. Each click performs one abstract instruction, not gate propagation or hardware clock timing.
steps: Use PP to select an instruction from instruction memory.
Decode the operation and select an immediate or memory operand.
Compute or route the value, then update ACC or memory as required.
Choose PP+1 or a jump target, using the zero flag for JZ.

label: 08 / Presentation
title: From classical bits to qubits.
subtitle: Group presentation / Quantum computers
summary: Explore the archived presentation and a new two-qubit Bell-circuit demonstration.
work: presentation_final.pptx credits Hamza Hafeez and Kanageshwaran DK. It discusses quantum concepts, architecture, applications and limitations, with a reference list. The archive also includes two legacy PPT variants and an AI-exploration outline.
review: The deck contains template attribution placeholders and claims that need qualification. String theory is not required to explain quantum computing; physical machines have finite qubit counts; entanglement does not permit faster-than-light messaging. Company examples remain historical claims from the archived slides, not verified current capabilities. The AI outline is labeled separately. The Bell circuit is newly created for this portfolio and runs locally as ideal state-vector arithmetic.
steps: Start two qubits in |00⟩.
Apply H to the first qubit, creating equal amplitudes for |00⟩ and |10⟩.
Apply CNOT, controlled by the first qubit, to obtain (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2.
A computational-basis measurement has 50% probability for 00 and 50% for 11 in this ideal model.
